documents.unit: KU Artificial Intelligence (ai.ku.edu, university AI task force)
documents.title: Guidance for Instructors
documents.summary: Page of suggested guidance for KU instructors: choose whether to use GenAI, state expectations in the syllabus, remind students of integrity duties, avoid AI detectors, and use CTE resources.
documents.stance_why: KU Guidance for Instructors says instructors 'may choose to teach about or use' GenAI 'as appropriate to the course, level, and discipline' and only suggests guidelines; it sets no rule of its own, so the decision sits with instructors.

units.why: The page opens by saying KU 'supports thoughtful use of AI to enrich course content', a welcoming stance toward AI in teaching, which fits P02 as a general welcome rather than a rule for a specific use.
units.anchor: KU supports thoughtful use of AI to enrich course content, support instructional goals, and streamline
units.policy: KU supports thoughtful use of AI to enrich course content, support instructional goals, and streamline routine tasks.

units.why: 'This guidance reflects the university's values of collaboration, equity, excellence, integrity, and respect' states the principles behind the guidance, so it is a framework statement (P56), not a rule.
units.anchor: This guidance reflects the university’s values of collaboration, equity, excellence, integrity, and respect.

units.why: 'Instructors may choose to teach about or use Generative AI (GenAI) tools as appropriate to the course, level, and discipline' leaves use to each instructor, so P04 (instructor sets the rule).
units.anchor: Instructors may choose to teach about or use Generative AI (GenAI) tools as appropriate to
units.policy: Instructors may choose to teach about or use Generative AI (GenAI) tools as appropriate to the course, level, and discipline.

units.why: 'Communicate expectations to students about coursework and the use of GenAI tools' with 'statements in the course syllabus' is a suggestion that instructors state AI expectations, matching P09 (modality should since the page says guidelines are 'suggested').
units.anchor: Communicate expectations to students about coursework and the use of GenAI tools.

units.why: 'Remind students of academic integrity obligations, including the practical consequences of academic integrity violations' tells instructors to communicate integrity duties and consequences; no type covers reminding students of consequences specifically (P36 classifies misuse, P37 states penalties), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Remind students of academic integrity obligations
units.uncovered_note: Instructors remind students of their academic integrity obligations and the consequences of violations.

units.why: 'Use of GenAI plagiarism detection tools is not recommended, as their accuracy is not guaranteed' advises against relying on detectors, which is P39.
units.anchor: Use of GenAI plagiarism detection tools is not recommended

units.why: 'may produce false positives and may introduce bias against non-native English speakers and students with disabilities' gives the equity and accuracy reason detectors are unreliable; fits P39 (unreliable detectors) rather than P53 because it is the detector rationale.
units.anchor: may produce false positives and may introduce bias against non-native English speakers and students with
units.policy: GenAI plagiarism checkers (such as Turnitin or GPTZero) may produce false positives and may introduce bias against non-native English speakers and students with disabilities.

units.why: 'CTE provides extensive guidance on adapting courses to generative AI' describes support for instructors (syllabus language, integrity, ethics, prompting), so P63.
units.anchor: provides extensive guidance on adapting courses to generative AI.

units.why: 'CTE has also developed AI related instructional modules available through Canvas' that instructors may request offers resources on AI risks and prompting; the audience is instructors who may use them, so P63 (faculty support). It also covers student-facing AI literacy, so the fit is partial.
units.anchor: CTE has also developed AI related instructional modules available through Canvas.
units.fit_note: the modules teach AI literacy (what AI is, risks, prompting, future of work) that instructors can use with students, which P63 (faculty-only support) does not capture; P70 is the alternative.

documents.title: Guidance for Students
documents.summary: Student-facing guidance: AI can help learning but must not replace the student's effort, students follow each instructor's rules, verify and own output, cite when required, protect privacy, and existing integrity rules still apply.
documents.stance_why: The student guide says KU 'does not currently have a university wide policy specific to the use of generative artificial intelligence' and that 'each instructor may have different guidelines'; students must follow each course's rules, so the stance is delegated to instructors.

units.why: 'KU supports the thoughtful use of AI to enhance educational experiences' is a general welcome of AI for students, P02.
units.anchor: KU supports the thoughtful use of AI to enhance educational experiences, support student research, and
units.policy: KU supports the thoughtful use of AI to enhance educational experiences, support student research, and assist with routine academic tasks.

units.why: 'Some instructors have integrated generative AI into assignments, while others restrict or prohibit its use' describes that rules differ by instructor, P04.
units.anchor: Some instructors have integrated generative AI into assignments, while others restrict or prohibit its use.

units.why: 'Because expectations may differ from one course to another, it is important to understand the guidance for each class' tells students to learn each course's rules: P78 (not P10, which is about asking when unsure).
units.anchor: it is important to understand the guidance for each class

units.why: 'ask your instructor for clarification if you are unsure' is P10 (ask when unsure).
units.anchor: ask your instructor for clarification if you are unsure

units.why: 'preparing students to engage thoughtfully with AI in their future careers' is named as a key focus, a career rationale (P44); the sentence also names academic integrity, so the fit is partial.

units.fit_note: the sentence names careers and academic integrity as two focus areas without saying students must learn AI skills.

units.why: 'its ability not just to support student work, but potentially to replace a student's own effort' explains why AI is risky for learning, P41.
units.anchor: potentially to replace a student’s own effort

units.policy: Generative AI creates text, images, code, and other content based on instructions or prompts provided in natural language.

units.policy: Generative AI can support learning by helping explain complex topics, providing examples, or generating practice questions.

units.anchor: AI should support your academic work, not do the work for you.

units.policy: A primary concern is relying on generative AI to replace your own thinking and effort rather than using it as a supplemental tool.

units.anchor: Improper use of generative AI may result in plagiarism or other forms of academic misconduct.

units.anchor: It is your responsibility to understand and follow the expectations for each course.

units.anchor: cite AI use when required by your instructor

units.anchor: Avoid entering personal information or information about others into AI tools.

units.why: 'Information shared with AI systems may be stored or reused by providers' explains the privacy risk, P50.
units.anchor: Information shared with AI systems may be stored or reused by providers.

units.why: 'does not currently have a university wide policy specific to the use of generative artificial intelligence' states there is no university rule and implies instructor-level rules, P04.
units.anchor: does not currently have a university wide policy specific to the use of generative artificial
units.policy: The University of Kansas does not currently have a university wide policy specific to the use of generative artificial intelligence in teaching and learning.

units.why: 'Existing expectations for academic integrity continue to apply when AI tools are used' ties AI use to existing policy, P77.
units.anchor: Existing expectations for academic integrity continue to apply when AI tools are used.

documents.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) Guidelines
documents.summary: Campus-wide GenAI principles for all users: definition of GenAI and AI, responsibility for outputs, verification, routine-assistance disclosure exemption, compliance with law and policy, data protection, research disclosure, and prohibited malware or spam uses. Only the course-specific clause is about teaching directly.

units.policy: A category of artificial intelligence, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) refers to tools designed to create new content based on patterns learned from the data used to train them.

documents.title: Maintaining academic integrity in the AI era
documents.summary: Teaching-center guidance: no AI-specific KU policy, so Senate Rules on misconduct apply; instructors are urged to write a class policy, permit AI where appropriate, talk and co-create with students, rely on reflection rather than detectors, redesign assignments, and plan faculty support. Includes two sample syllabus statements and a sample teacher letter.
documents.stance_why: The CTE page says KU 'does not have a specific policy about use of generative artificial intelligence' and 'encourage[s] faculty members to include a statement about permissible use'; it advises instructors but leaves the rule to each class.

units.policy: The University of Kansas does not have a specific policy about use of generative artificial intelligence in teaching and learning.

units.policy: Academic misconduct by a student shall include, but not be limited to, disruption of classes; threatening an instructor or fellow student in an academic setting; giving or receiving of unauthorized aid on examinations or in the preparation of notebooks, themes, reports or other assignments; knowingly misrepresenting the source of any academic work; unauthorized changing of grades; unauthorized use of University approvals or forging of signatures; falsification of research results; plagiarizing of another's work; violation of regulations or ethical codes for the treatment of human and animal subjects; or otherwise acting dishonestly in research.

notes: Coder A. Sample syllabus statements on the CTE pages (journalism, business, nursing, English, ME 208) are coded as policies because they state concrete rules, though they are examples and not KU-wide rules. Several sample statements repeat across the two CTE pages and are coded once per document. The HNRS 190 sample is from an honors course, not computing.
